questions.question: Which monitor does a thread acquire when it calls the synchronized instance method `void show()` on an object `test`?
options: A private lock that belongs only to the `show()` method
The monitor of `test` (the `this` object), the same one used by every other synchronized instance method of `test`
The monitor of `Test.class`, shared by all `Test` objects
A global JVM lock that pauses all other threads while `show()` runs
questions.explanation: Locks belong to objects, not to methods. A synchronized instance method is equivalent to wrapping its body in `synchronized (this) { ... }`. So every synchronized instance method of the same object competes for the same monitor. `ClassName.class` is used only by static synchronized methods, and synchronization never pauses unrelated threads.

questions.question: In `Demo2`, `Test` has two synchronized instance methods, `m1()` and `m2()`, and each one sleeps for 2 seconds. Thread-1 is inside `test.m1()` when Thread-2 calls `test.m2()` on the SAME object. What happens to Thread-2?
options: It enters `m2()` at once, because `m2()` is a different method from `m1()`
It enters `m2()` at once, because Thread-1 is sleeping and a sleeping thread gives up its lock
It waits (BLOCKED) until Thread-1 leaves `m1()`, because both methods need the monitor of `test`
It throws `IllegalMonitorStateException`, because the monitor is already owned
questions.explanation: Different synchronized instance methods on the same object share one monitor, so Thread-2 is blocked until Thread-1 releases it by leaving `m1()`. `sleep()` does not release the monitor. A blocked thread just waits for the monitor and no exception is thrown.

questions.question: Two threads call `b1.m1()` on the same `Bank` object at about the same time. What happens?
options: Both threads can be inside the block at the same time, because each call locks a brand-new object
Only one thread can be inside at a time, because the block is synchronized
The code does not compile, because `synchronized` needs a field or `this`
The second thread deadlocks, because the first thread's lock object is never released
questions.explanation: Threads only exclude each other if they synchronize on the SAME object. `new Object()` makes a different monitor on every call, so each thread acquires its own lock right away. Both 'Entered' lines can print before either 'Exiting' line. The fix is a single shared `private final Object lock`. Any object expression is legal inside `synchronized(...)`.

questions.question: `t1` runs `test.m1()` and `t2` runs `test.m2()` on the same `test` object. Can the output be `m1 entered`, `m2 entered`, `m1 exit`, `m2 exit`?
options: Yes: `m1()` locks the `Test.class` object and `m2()` locks the `test` object, which are different monitors
No: `m1()` is called through `test`, so it locks `test` like `m2()` does
No: a class lock also locks every instance of that class
Yes, but only when `t2` is started before `t1`
questions.explanation: `Test.class` is a separate object from any `Test` instance, so it has its own monitor. Calling a static method through an instance reference does not change that, because there is still no `this`. The two methods therefore do not block each other and their output can interleave. A class-level lock does not lock instances.

questions.question: In `class Service { synchronized void methodA() { methodB(); } synchronized void methodB() { ... } }`, a thread calls `service.methodA()`. What happens when it reaches the call to `methodB()`?
options: It deadlocks on itself, because it is waiting for a monitor it already holds
It releases the monitor first, then re-acquires it for `methodB()`, so another thread can slip in between
It throws `IllegalMonitorStateException`, because a monitor can be held only once
It enters `methodB()` immediately, because monitors are reentrant; the JVM counts the holds and releases the monitor after both methods exit
questions.explanation: Java monitors are reentrant. A thread that already owns `this`'s monitor can acquire it again, and the JVM increments a hold count instead of blocking. The monitor is fully released only after the outermost synchronized region exits. Without reentrancy, the first option (self-deadlock) would happen.

questions.question: `OrderService` has `private static int totalOrders;` and a method `synchronized void record() { totalOrders++; }`. Each worker thread creates its own `new OrderService()` and calls `record()`. The total still comes out too low. What is the correct fix?
options: Mark `totalOrders` as `final`, so that it cannot be overwritten
Make `record()` `static synchronized` (or lock on `OrderService.class`), so every thread uses the same class monitor
Add a second `synchronized` keyword inside `record()` to lock it twice
Call `Thread.yield()` after `totalOrders++` so the threads take turns
questions.explanation: A synchronized instance method locks `this`. Each thread uses a different `OrderService` object, so each thread gets a different monitor and nothing stops them from running at the same time. Static state needs a lock that all instances share, such as the `OrderService.class` monitor used by static synchronized methods. `final` would stop the field from being incremented at all.

questions.question: Why should a dedicated lock object usually be declared as `private final Object lock = new Object();`?
options: `private` stops outside code from synchronizing on it and blocking the class; `final` stops the reference from being replaced, which would split threads across different monitors
`private final` objects are created in a special memory area where locking is faster
`final` makes every field the lock protects immutable, so no other synchronization is needed
Without `private final`, the JVM refuses to use the object as a monitor
questions.explanation: If the lock were public, any outside code could hold it and stall the class. If the field were not final, reassigning it (for example `lock = new Object()`) could leave some threads locking the old object and others the new one, with no mutual exclusion between them. `final` applies only to the lock reference, not to the protected data, and any object can serve as a monitor.

questions.question: You review two classes. `Bank` has `deposit()` doing `balance += amount` under `synchronized (depositLock)`, and `withdraw()` doing `balance -= amount` under `synchronized (withdrawLock)`. `AccountManager` has `updateBalance()` doing `balance += amount` under `synchronized (accountLock)`, and `recordAuditEntry()` doing `auditEntries++` under `synchronized (auditLock)`. Which assessment is correct?
options: Both are correct, because every method that touches shared state is synchronized
Both are broken, because a class should never use more than one lock object
`Bank` is broken, because `deposit` and `withdraw` change the same `balance` under different locks; `AccountManager` is fine, because its two locks guard independent fields
`AccountManager` is broken, because two locks can run at the same time; `Bank` is fine, because deposits and withdrawals are different operations
questions.explanation: Data that is part of the same consistency rule must be guarded by the same lock. In `Bank`, a deposit and a withdrawal can run at the same time and overwrite each other's update to `balance`. `AccountManager`'s two locks protect unrelated fields, so letting those methods run concurrently is safe and reduces contention. Having a `synchronized` keyword on every method is not enough; what matters is which monitor guards which data.

questions.question: Two threads each call `Counter.increment()` once at about the same time. What is printed, and roughly how long does it take before both lines appear?
options: `1` then `1`, both after about 2 seconds, because the threads sleep in parallel
`2` then `2`, after about 2 seconds, because both increment before either prints
`1` then `2`, after about 2 seconds, because `sleep()` releases the class lock
`1` then `2`, with the second line about 2 seconds after the first (about 4 seconds in total)
questions.explanation: Both threads need the single `Counter.class` monitor, so the whole block, including the sleep, runs one thread at a time. The first thread sleeps, increments to 1 and prints 1. Then the second thread acquires the lock, sleeps again, increments to 2 and prints 2. `sleep()` keeps the monitor, so the two 2-second sleeps happen one after the other, not in parallel.

questions.question: Thread-1 is inside `synchronized (lock) { ... }` when its code throws an uncaught `RuntimeException`. Thread-2 is waiting to enter a block synchronized on the same `lock`. What happens?
options: Thread-2 stays BLOCKED forever, because Thread-1 died without releasing the monitor
The JVM releases the monitor as the exception propagates out of the block, so Thread-2 can acquire it
The exception is passed on to Thread-2, because it is waiting on the same monitor
The monitor is released only when garbage collection reclaims Thread-1's `Thread` object
questions.explanation: A monitor is released whenever execution leaves a synchronized region, whether it completes normally or ends with an exception. This automatic release is a key advantage of `synchronized` over manual `lock()`/`unlock()`, where forgetting a `finally` can leave the lock held forever. Exceptions are never passed to other threads.
